This research introduces a novel time series model called TV-PARX, which is based on a non-homogeneous Poisson process to model count data that exhibits dynamic patterns that change over time and may have underlying structures that shift unexpectedly. To account for these changes, the model utilizes a time-varying coefficient that is smoothed using a local constant kernel method, while a backfitting algorithm is employed to estimate the model parameters. The validity of the TV-PARX model is supported by establishing the consistency of the estimated time-varying coefficients and asymptotic normality of the estimated smoothing parameter. To evaluate the model's performance, Monte Carlo simulations are conducted, and a real-world application is carried out on Internet packet data to demonstrate its effectiveness.

On September 16, 2020, two Astrometric Telemetry Radiation networks, the ALL-SKY CAMERA-ASTRONOMY system and the WIDE-FIELD TELESCOPE instrument, carried out a field experiment to test the capabilities of wide-field photometry in determining the vertical aerosol optical depth over broad areas, eliminating the need for absolute calibration. The ALL-SKY CAMERA-ASTRONOMY system, located in Las Palma, Canary Islands, and the WIDE-FIELD TELESCOPE system in Mauna Loa, Hawaii, monitored the sun and a bright star, Achernar, throughout the day. By comparing the achernar photometry readings to the sun photometry measurements from a CE318 nephelometer, the all-sky camera astronomy system was found to have a precision of 0.03 within a broad wavelength range of 380 to 1020 nm. The wide-field telescope system showed a slightly lower precision of 0.05 across the 380 to 590 nm spectrum. Both systems demonstrated that wide-field photometry can effectively determine the aerosol optical depth over extensive areas without the need for absolute calibration, and that all-sky all-wavelength photometry is a viable instrument for monitoring the environment.

This study compares three molecular dynamics simulation methods—Langevin dynamics and two Hamiltonian approaches, STET and AHM, for exploring a biomolecular system's phase space, specifically an peptide like alanine dipeptide. We examine the methods' efficiency, accuracy, and how well they preserve the system's energy and oscillate around the true phase space distribution. Additionally, we examine the stability of these algorithms under various time steps and temperature settings. Our findings indicate that AHM outperforms both STET and LD in terms of efficiency and accuracy while maintaining good energy preservation and sampling characteristics. We also discuss the findings in the context of canonical sampling methods like MBPT and HBT, and highlight the importance of choosing the right simulation method based on the specific needs of molecular systems simulations.

This research presents new standards for creating training data for blind and visually impaired individuals, focusing on training artificial intelligence models for accurate image description. The initiative resulted in two publicly accessible datasets, one Western and one Chinese, comprising precisely described images suitable for training and testing AI models' capability to recognize images. The description guidelines developed serve as the foundation for evaluating these datasets and assessing the performance of the models trained on them. By assessing various existing AI models' performance on both datasets, the research aims to evaluate their effectiveness in replacing current evaluation methods, assisting researchers in assessing their models' ability to help visually impaired individuals.

This research focuses on an unconventional approach to an optimization problem within quantum field theory, specifically related to an anomaly equation that has been an area of debate since the 1970s. We utilize an intrinsic coordinate system in manifold domains and employ an innovative variational method inspired by fluid dynamics equations known as the Euler-Arnold equations. This variation leads to an explicit gradient descent algorithm, which we apply to the anomaly equation's optimization problem using a test function based on a free field theory model. Our numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and its potential for further research.

The interaction between heavy quarks, specifically charm and bottom, in a vertical motion through a vacuum is investigated using a simple theoretical model within the framework of Quantum Chromodynamics. In this study, heavy quarks are assumed to be independent initially and affected by both perturbative and non-perturbative aspects of QCD. The behavior of these interactions is analyzed by examining the survival probability of particle pairs. The results obtained from this research show that the model's predictions align well with current experimental data for both B mesons and D mesons in the jet fragmentation environment. Additionally, the results provide valuable information on the non-perturbative parameters involved.

This work investigates a fundamental communication system problem that aims to maximize fair-throughput while using a wideband signal that can be formed in multiple ways. The system has multiple receivers, each with its own reception quality in various formation configurations, and we consider a linear model to model throughputs. We show that the task of maximizing fair-throughput is equivalent to maximizing the product of throughputs, and we propose an algorithm to optimize the throughputs based on the fair-throughput target value. The algorithm guarantees an outcome close to the optimal fair-throughput within a specified time frame. We also analyze the complexity of the optimization task in relation to the number of possible configurations and show that it is computationally difficult in cases where there are many possible formations. As a bonus, our work provides new insights into the complexity of maximizing the product of throughputs for continuous and discrete signals.

The study examines the dglap evolution of parton distribution functions (pdfs) in a neural network-based model and a variational approach, comparing the outcomes before and after dglap evolution at a specific scale. A deep neural network based regression model is employed to learn the initial conditions for the variational approach and the values for the asymptotic dglap evolution. A Bayesian optimization framework is used to fit the model parameters to experimental data. The dglap evolution is critical as it allows the obtained pdfs to be applicable at various scales, and the benefits of this method's capabilities are demonstrated through a case study on the fitting of proton and neutron pdfs.

A new k-epsilon-based combustion model was developed and tested within a basic linearized framework to manage turbulent, reacting flows, utilizing an integral equation approach to derive a stability equation. To test the framework, two flame test cases were simulated with the newly created model and a previously established model, the Eddy Break-Up model, showing consistent results. To verify the models' accuracy, a high-order spectral method was used to solve the stability equation, comparing the results with a finite difference method used in a prevailing study, yielding nearly identical outcomes. Finally, global sensitivity analyses were conducted on the combining of the linearized Navier-Stokes equations and the linearized combustion equation, using both SVD and a local optimization approach, demonstrating the equivalence of the methods. Overall, the newly created model proved to be well-suited for the basic linearized framework, the proposed numerical method showed its effectiveness, and the sensitivity analysis revealed the viability of the optimization approach.

This paper proposes a revised interpretation of nonlocal gravity theory, derived from its original formulation by Wilfred van Flandern, showing direct correlation with observable quantities. By eliminating an inaccurate assumption within the theory, we arrive at nonlocal gravity equations that suggest long-range gravitational effects are inextricably linked to locally measurable mass distributions. Consequently, this reinterpreted model yields results consistent with general relativity, obviating the need for dark matter to explain gravitational phenomena and demonstrating its local nature.

A notable trend observed recently shows that higher multiplicity pp and pPb collisions exhibit behavior reminiscent of qqbarA interactions, particularly in terms of strange particle production and its variants, such as ks0, l-, and K-. To investigate this phenomenon, a model based on initial energy density was developed, positing that enhanced conditions could trigger a phase transition to quark gluon plasma within individual pp interactions. The predictions of this model align well with the noted trends when examined across various pp and pA scenarios, although further research is needed to validate the role of energy density and explore the characteristics of particle production and suppression, specifically rho0, k*0, f0(980), and f2(1270) within both pp and pA interactions.

A significant portion of the neutron star population within the Milky Way, particularly the inactive and partially accreting systems, has yet to be discovered. To address this, we employ a Bayesian inference approach, utilizing the known populations of X-ray and radio binaries with neutron stars to predict the number of N(LQX), systems that are similar to gigahertz radio pulsars. Our predictions are compared against the observed populations of both X-ray and radio binaries with neutron stars, as well as the predicted populations of stellar remnants from supernovae and neutron star mergers. We find that the formation rates of binary systems involving massive stars and those formed after a neutron star merges with another neutron star or white dwarf are in good agreement with the observed and predicted populations. However, we note that a constant formation rate from massive star birth does not adequately explain the established millisecond radio pulsar population within the Galaxy. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose a time-varying formation rate from the birth of massive stars, a recurrent accretion phase following the birth of a binary system with two neutron stars, and a more in-depth examination of the characteristics of the N(LQX) system once it is found.

A bipartite graph can be represented in a planar manner by dividing a vertex with degree $d$ into $d-1$ parts and adding edges between them in one second-level approach. Conversely, a more complex method involves modifying the graph by increasing a vertex's degree by creating new ones and adding edges, then applying the second-level approach to this altered graph.

Degrading memory performance through the introduction of cache misses and evictions has emerged as a technique for enhancing Flush+Reload attacks by reducing the need for large numbers of measurements. While previous methods focusing on optimizing cache performance have been limited to specific architectures like Intel and AMD processors, this research introduces HyperDegrade, a system that works effectively on virtual machines and has demonstrated greater efficacy than both degrading and modifying cache performance techniques. HyperDegrade combines the advantages of both approaches, allowing for the easy application of memory performance modifications through the introduction of misses and evictions. The source code for HyperDegrate is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/itaykashani/HyperDegrade.

A new variant of the traditional 2-brick model is introduced, called the diagonal-brick model, where bricks can move diagonally. It's demonstrated that this updated model retains the capacity to replicate any arbitrarily knotted structure, just as the original model did with bricks moving parallel to the x and y axes. Moreover, the article proves that the diagonal-brick model can also integrate with the previously established knotted structures by combining them with 3D-printed, arbitrarily knoved x and y-aligned bars. Consequently, it's shown that the diagonal-brick model on its own can form any possible knotted configuration when considered in relation to these bars, all without the need for additional bars or models.

The study examines how two types of learning algorithms, fixed and adaptable threshold strategies, function within a cooperative multi-agent setup called the "tug-of-war" problem. This scenario involves a group of agents trying to tip the balance in their favor by performing actions that cost resources but increase the likelihood of success, all while managing limited resources and uncertain action outcomes. A key factor in this study is the task difficulty distribution, with both uniform and non-uniform patterns examined. Through a series of experiments, the performance of the strategies is evaluated based on the amount of resources consumed and the success rate achieved, revealing that in straight-forward cases, fixed threshold strategies work well, but more complex situations call for the flexibility of adaptable strategies. Notably, the research highlights the importance of the task difficulty distribution in determining the best approach and provides useful insights for both theoretical understanding and practical applications of collective decision-making processes.

We explore specific scenarios where certain subsets of a product space are identified as Cartesian components, focusing on the role of symmetry groups in these arrangements. We introduce a unified framework that encompasses regular group actions, actions by diagonal groups, and combinations of these actions as well as actions by generalized diagonal groups. A key byproduct of our analysis is the determination of the size of the component set for arrangements acted upon by generalized diagonal groups and generalized wreath products. Our findings for generalized wreath products are extended to generalized dihedral products. A code exemplaring actions by generalized dihedral products is constructed, and we provide exact calculations of the component set size for structures formed by generalized dihedral products, even when involving multiple distinct diagonal groups.

This research introduces a novel design, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, derived from the conventional Sagnac setup, demonstrating its capacity to achieve long effective arm lengths through simple extensions. A theoretical model has been developed to predict the behavior of this new design and the results confirm its validity. The sloshing-Sagnac design offers advantages over the conventional Sagnac design by mitigating the limitations of laser power and optical recycling, showing potential for enhanced sensitivity through simple extensions.

This study introduces an enhanced version of a novel NOVR-XL protocol designed for XL-MIMO systems to address efficiency issues in scenarios with heavy user loads. Our proposed NOVR-XL protocol makes intelligent use of initial access information to minimize unnecessary retries and compares NOVR-XL and NOVRXL+ protocols with traditional random access methods in a realistic field of view (FOV) scenario. Our simulation results show that the enhanced version of the novel protocol outperforms the revised NOVR-XL protocol and significantly improves the performance of standard random access protocols, particularly in densely populated areas.

This research addresses the limitations of both standalone $n$-gram and neural language models by developing a hybrid approach. The proposed method utilizes a deep neural network, specifically an encoder-decoder transformer, to predict the outcomes of $n$-grams. A variation of the standard training objective is then implemented to learn a mapping between the outputs of the neural model and the final probabilities. Our hybrid model demonstrates enhanced performance in machine translation tasks, showing improved results in low-resource scenarios and when dealing with text that has significant domain differences.

This research project focuses on enhancing the accuracy of an OCR system used to analyze election ballots in Canada. The primary goal was to minimize errors caused by the graphical representation of choices on ballots and to ensure that the system's output matched the statistical quality of manual counting methods. An IEEE standard governing the equivalence of automatic and manual counting processes served as a framework for the project. The proposed solution involves a three-step process: initially, Tesseract, an open-source OCR library, is used to transcribe the ballot images. The transcription is then adjusted to correct common errors and account for the specific ballot design, with help from an automated system and a database. Finally, the data collected is analyzed. A key component of this process is the correction database, which is built using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. The system was tested on provincial election results from Quebec, and the outcomes were evaluated based on the variability of the data. The proposed method demonstrated a level of accuracy that was on par with the official results provided by election authorities.

This study investigates the circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere modified with initial conditions resembling those of a Martian storm, specifically a baroclinic event on Mars reported in November 2001. When the Earth-like atmosphere is left without external forces, it develops a general circulation pattern that mirrors the typical Earth pattern. However, when conservative heating is applied to mimic the extreme temperature differences seen in the Martian storm, the atmosphere reconfigures into a pattern strikingly similar to the specific Mars storm observed. Two3D models, the GFDL and the MHD, yield comparable outcomes. The research highlights that both large-scale weather events on Mars and disturbances generated in computer simulations share common characteristics. These features include a low-latitude warm air bubble, a high-latitude cool air bubble, and mid-latitude wind patterns driven by temperature contrasts, demonstrating the ease with which baroclinic storms can form in atmospheric models. The findings also provide valuable insights for the future Mars atmosphere mission, the FMA.

This paper introduces a novel representation of functional spaces that is particularly suitable for machine learning applications. It begins with the Hankel path integral formulation of the Gamma function, leading to a complex-valued vector space that is valid for all parameter values. It then describes a learning algorithm that allows for the estimation of any special function, including the Gamma function, by utilizing simple neural network architectures with basic activation functions.

This research introduces a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method for quantum field theory that easily integrates with existing classical hydrodynamic simulations to handle strong quantum fluctuations. Our linearized approach is validated through applications and comparisons with full simulations, specifically examining the first-order quantum Coriolis effects on fast-expanding relativistic fluids and suddenly expanded fluids that reach a steady state. Additionally, our method enables precise simulations of suddenly expanded quantum fluids with varying initial conditions, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting oscillations known as Artounde sound and verifying the linearized hydrodynamic equations' accuracy under small gradients. Our quantum hydrodynamic scheme also enables simulations of freely expanding relativistic fluids that respect initial conditions with classical and quantum descriptions, revealing discrepancies between the two approaches over time and allowing precise calculations of entropy growth due to the quantization of vortical flows. Ultimately, our method provides a powerful tool for investigating the quantum vacuum's inherent properties through laboratory experiments with relativistic heavy ion colliders.

Teacher-Student learning frameworks have proven effective in reducing the size of deep neural networks while maintaining their performance, with the large capacity of an expansive teacher network guiding the student network's representation learning. Although Teacher-Student architectures are widely used, particularly in visual classification, many existing teacher networks fail to fully exploit their potential due to computational constraints. To address this limitation, we introduce a high-capacity teacher network, CapsNet-2GL, built upon the powerful Capsule networking structure and enhanced with a global linear relation to provide richer context information. To enable an efficient training process for the substantial CapsNet-2GL teacher network, we employ an iterative kronecker-gradient computation method that allows for more accurate gradient calculation and a larger update step size, benefiting the student network's performance. Experiments on standard image datasets demonstrate that various lightweight student networks, sharing architectural characteristics with the CapsNet-2GL teacher network, achieve superior accuracy in visual classification and balance point prediction compared to multiple widespread teacher networks.

To effectively manage complex, real-world problems involving large-scale graphical models, we need advanced methods that can work with the full model specification. Bucket elimination serves this purpose by providing a systematic way to analyze the graphical structure and handle both inference and optimization tasks. This process operates similarly to variable elimination but produces a concise representation of the remaining factors, which can be an integer linear program for optimization problems or a discrete probability distribution for inference. Using the same algorithm with the complete model specification allows us to accurately predict the model's structure and properties, including identifying cyclic substructures and assessing the efficiency of different random walk approaches. This capability enables the creation of customized random walk models that work efficiently on the entire model specification.

Determining whether integer coefficients can be derived from the formal power series expansion of the Hilbert-Poincaré for centralizers of subalgebras is an unresolved issue in mathematics. Specifically, we address the problem of determining if the coefficients of the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be obtained from the $(q,\zeta)$ expansion. By utilizing an integer coefficient recurrence relation, we establish that the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrackl_2)$ has integer coefficients for all $n$ greater than or equal to 0. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of finding similar recurrence relations for centralizers of other subalgebras such as $(so3)$ and $(gl1)$, as well as their composited subalgebras, to determine their Hilbert-Poincaré series.

Statistical significance assessments can be performed using paired-permutation tests via two methods: an established approximate Monte Carlo approach and an newly developed precise calculation method. While the Monte Carlo approach is computationally efficient, the exact method offers definitive results. Our novel exact algorithm significantly improves upon previous methodologies by utilizing an efficient calculation of factorials' greatest common divisors, allowing for rapid determination of exact p-values. Notably, our method reduces computation time compared to the established algorithm starting from 1000 samples, and demonstrates substantial savings at higher sample sizes, making the exact approach practically feasible.

The observation that individual non-Abelian forces, specifically the strong and weak interactions, exhibit analogous behavior when examining particle flows in transverse momentum, applies to comparing transverse momentum dependencies of elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) flow coefficients from identified hadrons produced in heavy ion collisions. A unified framework is presented that fits both $v_2$ and $v_3$ coefficients from various hadron types in Au+Au and Pb+Pb collisions by utilizing only the constituent quark masses as initial conditions for the Lund string model to calculate hadron production within the EPOS LHC framework. A Fritiof-like approach is utilized to model hadronization, with a focus on string melting and hadronization processes. Although a perfect unification of the $v_2$ and $v_3$ distributions is not achieved, the current model demonstrates that both flows can be described using nearly identical parameters for both strong and weak interactions, indicating the possibility of unifying the descriptions of hadron production in heavy ion collisions for both QCD and EWK scenarios with further refinement.

This paper addresses the challenge of detecting and estimating the position of targets within a specific area, particularly when using a sensor with restricted observation capabilities. A Bayesian approach is employed to model the targets, and a control algorithm is developed to minimize the expected number of targets within the area by strategically moving the sensor. A key contribution of this research is the re-calculation of the control problem's dynamic programming values, enabling the detection of targets that current methods assume are already within the sensor's field of view when the sensor moves. This modification allows for more accurate target estimation and reduces the expected number of targets, even with targets that are initially undetected. A case study utilizing real data from the MAVEN mission to investigate the atmosphere of Mars validates the proposed approach.

Machine learning techniques have significantly impacted various sports analytics fields including basketball, American football, and ice hockey. In soccer though, the predominance of chance-based actions like fouls, goal kicks, and throw-ins complicates the application of these methods. This research introduces a free playing AI agent developed through deep reinforcement learning with a game model, demonstrating its success in a simulated soccer environment by achieving a 60% victory rate against a basic strategy and a 30% victory rate against a more sophisticated strategy. The research also utilizes this AI to analyze specific game scenarios and compares its actions to those recommended by existing analyses.

This paper presents an automated laboratory system designed for remote physics experiments, responding to the needs created by the COVID-19 pandemic. The system integrates an EPOC device, Jupyter Notebook, and Python libraries to enable telework-enabled research and development of new experimental physics setups. By utilizing pre-built containers with pre-configured software, the system simplifies the process of establishing a functional experimental laboratory within a few days. The open-source nature of the system encourages wider adoption and utilization among the scientific community, with over 100 downloads and positive feedback from users who found it useful for various experiments and educational purposes. The system's source code and documentation are available on GitHub for further exploration and use.

This study investigates the stability of solitary wave solutions in a specific type of anharmonic oscillator system with an anharmonic term of the second kind, focusing on the system's behavior under certain conditions where the anharmonic term is small and the system is subject to an external force that does not decay as time progresses. Building on previous research, we demonstrate that sufficiently stable solitary wave solutions within this system maintain their integrity over extended periods of time. A key component of our analysis involves examining the stability of these solutions within the anharmonic oscillator system and developing a corrected version of the invariant manifold found in the harmonic oscillator system with respect to the non-zero external force. As a note, proving the orbital stability of these solitary wave solutions in this specific anharmonic oscillator system is more complex compared to systems where the anharmonic term is small and the system is subject to initial disturbances that do not decay as time progresses.

The effectiveness of searches for particles that are difficult to detect, specifically neutral long-lived particles (NLSPs), varies considerably based on the decay distance of the particle. For decay lengths that are short, the technique is comparable to the standard search for sparticles that decay immediately, such as squarks and gluinos. On the other hand, decay lengths that are long result in particles that are lost within the collider machine, making them undetectable. In between these extremes, within the range from 1 centimeter to 10 kilometers, the absence of signals from produced NLSPs that are charged leads to the most significant constraints. This absence necessitates more innovative detection methods, such as those proposed for detectors installed close to be placed near the main beam pipe of the LHC.

This study examines the role of context in semantic shifts by comparing two contextual sources, social media and dictionaries, to analyze entries related to COVID-19 that emerged between 2020 and 2021. Using a corpus of Google Books data from 2009 to 2019, researchers identified and evaluated contextual variations through the Application of Contextual Variance Encoder (CVE) to classify semantic changes. Initially, the study aimed to quantify the connection between contextual variation and semantic distance, but it found that shifts in context do not always indicate semantic evolution. However, drawing on real-world examples influenced by COVID-19, the research proposes that contextual shifts can lead to semantic changes without necessarily doing so. Ultimately, the study finds that contextual variations caused by the pandemic result in lower average scores on the WordNet database, as well as a higher frequency of new meanings added through Urban Dictionary compared to changes in how words are used on Twitter.

Researchers have discovered an unusual pattern in the movement of distant galaxies, suggesting the possible existence of a very light quantum field with mass between $10^{-28}$ and $10^{-26}$ eV. This finding is impactful, but before we can estimate the characteristics of dark matter, we must first rule out the influence of heavier, slightly more dense particles, such as those with masses around 10^-1 and 10^-2 eV. Current data from the cosmic microwave background, the distribution of galaxies, and the intense radiation of quasars indicates that these intermediate-density particles make up less than a few percent of the total dark matter. While the specifics of the under-explored under-the-curve section of the dark matter composition spectrum are still unclear, reasonable estimates place the limit at around 10^-3 of dark matter. Therefore, even if we assume the existence of multiple, distinct ultralight fields, the predominant component is still likely to be too heavy for even the most creative proposals, likely exceeding 10^-2 eV. At this point, the search for this heavier particle becomes inextricably linked to the search for the primary constituent of dark matter.

This research delves into the use of coherent states as approximations within the mean-field framework for driven quantum systems, with a focus on harmonic oscillators and spin systems under a constant driving force with or without structured dissipation. We conduct a rigorous stability analysis of these states when used as solutions to these systems' equations of motion, with a detailed examination of driven harmonic oscillators with structured dissipation, both individually and in combination. A theoretical framework is developed to assess the validity of coherent states as reliable solutions for these systems, with a specific emphasis on Rabi oscillations in driven spin systems. A numerical algorithm is proposed to verify the validity conditions and assess the accuracy of coherent-state-based wavefunctions. Notable findings include the identification of situations where coherent states fail to accurately represent the system's state, with a specific example of a driven damped harmonic oscillator subject to a time-dependent force, and a detailed exploration of the decay of validity conditions in driven spin systems as the number of particles increases. The research also provides insights into the effectiveness of multi-site coherent states in mitigating non-linearities in spin systems and a justification for the rapid decay of validity conditions in these systems as the number of particles grows.

Quantum relational Hoare logic is used to describe specifying intermediate state information for end-user quantum programs that affect both input and output. This approach is particularly relevant when dealing programs with complex relationships between inputs and outputs, as opposed to simple transformation tasks. Our implementation provides a block for this type of specification and offers proofs for compositional rules that aid in the integration of these and other operations. These enhancements expand the capabilities of Quantum Hoare logic and contribute to the development of more advanced verification tools. These tools can effectively assess the correctness of programs that have been judged difficult, if not impossible, to evaluate previously. In addition, we have created an online resource at the following address: https://github.com/QuantumRelHoareLogic/QRHL.

The paper addresses the limitations of current vector magnetic field maps, which often neglect the influence of plasma properties on magnetic structure determination. By incorporating plasma data, particularly density and pressure, into magnetic field reconstructions, researchers can obtain more accurate 3D representations. A key focus of the paper is on utilizing the "bulk magnetogram" concept, which considers the magnetic fill fraction, to enhance field measurements. The authors present a workflow for integrating property data and utilizing the magnetic fill fraction to refine field maps, demonstrating the method's effectiveness through a case study of a sunspot group. The results reveal that accounting for magnetic fill fraction can significantly improve field divergence free solutions and obtain more realistic structures, particularly in low-fill fraction areas. The paper contributes to the development of advanced data pipelines and emphasizes the importance of incorporating plasma properties in vector magnetic field maps, paving the way for better understanding of magnetic structure and dynamics, particularly around active regions.

Wedges with restricted sections covered by spheres can be examined within Coxeter groups, using a large subset of simple reflections S' as the set from which words are formed. The process of word reduction is guided by the relation s^2 = 1. Our focus is on specific Coxeter groups, analyzing the scenario where the section's size is at most 1 and exploring the connection between the sphere count within the wedge and the size of S'. Through computational experiments with spherical and affine Coxeter groups, we've discovered that the linearity constant λ(W), representing the rate of wedge growth, equals 1 for both spherical and affine Coxeter groups. This implies that the number of spheres within a wedge is directly proportional to the section's size, with the constant of proportionality being 1. Our findings are supported by existing literature, showing agreement with established results and providing a deeper understanding of the structure within Coxeter groups. Notably, our approach offers a fresh geometric perspective on Deodhar's theorem, moving away from the traditional reflection generation method.

Bertrand curves are considered well-defined in Euclidean and Minkowski planes. This paper focuses on identifying and classifying Bertrand curves within the spherical plane S2 and hyperbolic plane H2. A key finding is that both in the spherical and hyperbolic planes, the concept of Bertrand curves reduces to that of circular arcs, contrasting with Euclidean and Minkowski planes where the definition varies. A specific condition is established for determining when circular arcs in the spherical plane can be classified as Bertrand curves, dependent on the chosen metric. A detailed characterization of Bertrand curves in the hyperbolic plane is provided, considering various metric representations. The research offers insights into the geometric properties and characteristics of these curves.

Multi-task learning aims to enable AI models to simultaneously learn from and master various related tasks. As the number of related tasks grows, it becomes increasingly important for all tasks to be equally represented. Otherwise, more prominent tasks might dominate the learning process. This issue is particularly critical when employing certain training methodologies, such as linear combinations of training objectives, and can lead to suboptimal model performance, especially with training goals that emphasize accurate prediction, like mean squared error. To address this challenge, we introduce a task embedding space that can be optimized using an objective function, such as KL Divergence, to ensure all tasks are equally represented. This approach is guaranteed to converge to a global optimum and can be computed in constant time per training step. Experiments on both visual and tabular data demonstrate that this method effectively balances training by reducing training goal dominance and promotes better learning across all tasks by at least 10% while maintaining optimization goals.

Programmatic synthetic tasks, exemplified by the creation of if-then rules, enable the neural networks to learn specific concepts without requiring a large amount of training data. This paper introduces a standalone approach for training a model to predict the structure of if-then relationships, which consists of conditions and actions, and also explores the advantages of training the model on the hierarchical organization of relation categories. A neural model named BERT is utilized in this process. Furthermore, a more complex structure is proposed, dividing conditions and actions into multiple classes and subclasses, and presents a hierarchical framework for these categories. The study's findings demonstrate that training the model on this hierarchical structure leads to improved generalization of the network and presents a fully functional if-then relation structure with nine main categories and a total of fourteen classes, along with a visual representation of the hierarchy.

To enable our network to output videos from unseen viewpoints, we adopted a framework that represents both seen and novel viewpoints in a dual manner. This approach allows our model to learn a connection between viewpoints in way that facilitates videos from novel viewpoints to be outputted in a manner that's consistent with seen viewpoints. Experiments conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this dual representation learning method.

This paper investigates a modified version of the graph metric known as the truncated geodesic distance, focusing on a specific threshold value $t$. When the distance between two nodes in a graph is within the threshold, it remains unchanged; however, any distance exceeding the threshold is considered equivalent to the threshold value itself. We examine how this modification affects the properties of the graph, particularly the dimension required to uniquely identify points within it. For a family of graph structures including paths, cycles, grids, and trees with limited branching factor, we determine the truncated dimension equivalent to the standard metric dimension. Additionally, we explore the changes in the truncated dimension when a constant factor is applied to the threshold value, revealing that for certain graphs like grids and grids with branching nodes, the dimension remains consistent beyond a certain threshold. A stochastic algorithm is proposed to determine the threshold at which the truncated dimension equals the metric dimension for any given graph.

This study introduces a novel approach for identifying various cardiac issues from auscultation sounds, even in noisy environments, by integrating a noise reduction technique with a deep learning-based classifier. The proposed method combines spectrum-transformed auscultation sounds and noise signals using the Little-Marsaglia-Branick (LMB) algorithm to generate mixed sounds, which are then fed into a neural network-based noise reduction model and a deep convolutional neural network-based classifier for obtaining the cleaned sounds and anomaly diagnosis results, respectively. The proposed method was evaluated using the PhysioNet/CinC 2017 dataset, which contains stethoscope records of normal hearts and hearts with anomalies, along with synthetic noise added through different techniques. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms other methods in terms of exception detection accuracy, particularly in challenging environments and with different types of noise. Additionally, the proposed method can be easily generalized to various noise types with minimal retraining, making it a powerful tool for accurate anomaly detection from auscultation sounds in real-world scenarios.

To investigate the role of low-density environments around extreme starburst galaxies, we analyzed data from 21 verified galaxies with HATSS 30um-selected starbursts that met specific criteria of SFR > 100 solar masses per year and BZM EB ratio > 0.1. These data helped us examine the relationships between CI fine structure line ratios, specifically [N II]86/48um, [O III]52um/88um, and [S III]33um/18um, as well as their connections with key parameters like BZM EB ratio, CI/BG ratio, and the f10.2 value. We observed distinct trends where an increased scarcity of a cold neutral gas reservoir and an abundance of circumgalactic gas, or an outflow, led to higher CI/BG ratios and adjusted CI fine structure line ratios. The shifts in CI fine structure ionization ratios occurred due to the dominance of hot, ionized winds and the deficiency of the cold neutral gas phase. Although the CI fine structure ratios showed some scatter, we found that the f10.2 - CI/BG ratio and the CI/BG - BZM EB ratio scatter could be reduced significantly, indicating the significant impact of circumgalactic gas outflows on the spectrum of extreme starburst galaxies.

This study investigates the movement of a second-class particle in ASEP on a one-dimensional grid with constant input and output rates. When environments around the particle are initially random and independent, we determine the velocity distribution of the second-class particle after a given time period. A method is also presented to calculate this velocity distribution for various initial conditions that are stepped and EKP, both with and without constant rates of flow. Additionally, the findings are extended to ASEP in higher dimensions and multi-colored models.

Data collected from field observations provides crucial insights into the parameters of interest for epidemiologists, although the utility of fitting differential models to such data requires careful consideration of its biological feasibility. We introduce a framework for converting such data into a format suitable for fitting differential models, complementing existing conversion methods with a smoother approach to obtain birth rates from reported SIR estimates. Applying this methodology to real-world data gathered in China and Sweden, we fit an SIR-based differential model to validate previously estimated parameter values, and fit an SEIR-based model to verify reasonable recovery and infection rate assumptions. Additionally, we utilize an SEIR-based differential model to estimate the basic reproduction number resulting from implementing social distancing measures in Sweden, demonstrating close alignment with estimates derived from an SIR-based compartmental model fitting. By integrating discrete and continuous approaches, we aim to develop robust methods for estimating desirable epidemiological parameter values from real-world data.

Observing a reddening of NUV-r colors as galaxy masses increase is confirmed across the stellar mass range of 10^9 to 10^11 solar masses for spheroidal components at z=0. However, above a threshold of approximately 10^10.3 solar masses, a bluer trend emerges for the most massive galaxies due to a surge in star-forming activity within their disks and the possible inclusion of non-bulge components in measurements. To mitigate this effect, we examined the NUV-r colors of the most massive galaxies's bulge regions only, revealing that the trend of increasing NUV-r colors with mass continues even beyond the previously noted turn-over point.

This research delves into the potential of using only source language metadata to learn a cross-lingual sentiment classification model, specifically for Turkish-German. The study aims to develop an unsupervised method that can transfer sentiment knowledge from a well-resourced language to a resource-limited one. Several strategies were evaluated, building upon existing techniques and creating a novel approach called NCME. The approaches were assessed on multiple datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of using source language metadata to learn cross-lingual sentiment models. The best-performing method, NCME, showed significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the research explored the impact of monolingual sentiment data and embedding models on model performance, providing valuable insights for future research.

Recently, an unusual rotation profile in KIC 9267654 was identified through global spectroscopic analyses. Initial data suggested a differential rotation pattern similar to that seen in Sun-like stars, with inner regions rotating faster than outer regions. However, further investigation revealed that differential ionization effects within the stellar atmosphere could potentially explain this profile without any actual differential rotation occurring. Despite this explanation, it is important to consider other possible explanations, including the influence of global magnetic fields on rotation measurements, although this seems unlikely given the lack of magnetic activity shown by the star. Ultimately, more observational data is needed to confirm the cause of this unusual rotation profile, although stellar winds and obliquation do not seem to be plausible explanations based on the star's characteristics.

Fake news poses serious threats to society, making its effective detection crucial. Although some false information mimics fake news by spreading misleading true events, this research focuses on genuine false narratives. While the rise of generative AI has given creators powerful tools to produce convincing fake content, it has also sparked the development of advanced detectors that use these very tools to identify such misinformation. Our proposed meta-learning based framework called MetaFEND emulates the creator-detector arms race, enabling the model to learn from available data and adapt to new false news stories with limited training time and resources. Experiments show that MetaFEND outperforms existing methods when faced with unseen fake news, and we demonstrate the model's capabilities by training it on distinct datasets to detect false narratives in various languages. Furthermore, the MetaFEND framework's ability to leverage AI-generated content to detect false news proves its potential for practical applications.

A quaternary Golay complementary array pair is considered in this study, with its feasibility conditions examined in detail. Initially, it was demonstrated that quaternary Golay complementary array pairs of length at most 12932 are feasible, building on existing results. Subsequently, two primary methods were explored: first, by extending real-valued complementary arrays to create quaternary Golay complementary array pairs, and second, through array concatenation techniques. As an outcome of this research, it was found that quaternary Golay complementary array pairs of length 10001 are not feasible, while feasibility was confirmed for lengths 10201, 10404, 10800, 10809, 11044, 11200, 11607, 11716, 11800, 12000, 12010, 12252, 12600, 12700, and 13000.

This research focuses on utilizing deep learning techniques, specifically using CNNs, to automatically identify and mark important areas in medical images, particularly in chest X-rays. The goal is to develop a system that can help with diagnosing pneumonia by utilizing region-based interest sampling and a two-part CNN-based architecture. The initial part of the architecture employs a generative approach to create regions of the images, while the second part classifies these regions to determine if they are important areas, such as indicating pneumonia. The system was tested on large datasets of chest X-ray images and found to be effective in identifying important areas in the images and useful for creating images that can be used for diagnosis purposes. The research also explored using the important areas created by the system to make images more easily classifiable using a classifier based on a three-layer neural network. Overall, the research demonstrates the potential of using deep learning techniques to analyze medical images and assist with diagnosing diseases such as pneumonia.

This work introduces an innovative framework called Joint Embedding Learning (JEL) that integrates both unsupervised and supervised approaches to feature extraction. The model starts with an initial, basic network architecture that progressively adds layers through an optimization process guided by an objective function with multiple components. The first component focuses on minimizing within-class variance by projecting data into a lower dimensional space, while the remaining components add supervised learning criteria in higher dimensional spaces. The approach is flexible and allows for the incorporation of various supervised learning criteria, such as maximum between-class variance, support vector machines, and neural networks. The method is evaluated through multiple experiments demonstrating its effectiveness.

Machine learning models that have been trained on knowledge graphs, specifically on factual triples, are emerging as a novel type of representation learning. Although there is already some research exploring the development of benchmarks and models pre-trained on these knowledge graphs, very little work has been done on creating learning frameworks that incorporate these triples and on creating pre-trained models that can be utilized for various tasks within the domain of language. This paper aims to bridge this gap by exploring the creation of a high-quality, large-scale factual triple dataset called CQKG, along with the design of a novel, effective framework that enables machine learning models to learn from both text-based and knowledge graph-based data. Furthermore, we conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the performance of pre-trained models on this new framework across multiple evaluation tasks, including knowledge graph extension, fact verification, and a wide range of factual questions within the field of applied mathematics and physics, demonstrating the effectiveness of these models and the value of the CQKG dataset.

This study investigates the influence of non-linear effects on a Yang-Mills charge parameter in a big black hole system with an extended horizon in de Sitter space. A modified master equation is derived to calculate the scattering probability of massless particles that do not behave linearly. Our findings reveal that non-linear effects result in a smaller shadow and a less intense thermal radiation pattern for big black holes with an anharmonic Yang-Mills charge. As the anharmonic coefficient increases, the disparity between the linear and non-linear thermal profiles and shadows of big black holes with an anharmonic Yang-Mills charge in de Sitter space becomes more pronounced. A striking correlation is found between the thermal profiles and the shape of the shadow of big black holes with an anharmonic Yang-Mills charge in de Sitter space. These findings could help confirm the presence of black holes in an anharmonic Yang-Mills charge state within an expandable horizon in de Sitter space and play a crucial role in validating the linear or non-linear behavior of particles through the analysis of the thermal profiles and shadow of black hole images.

Quantum phenomena such as entanglement enhancement and suppression are effectively illustrated within the context of optical tomograms, as opposed to traditional non-classical measures like entanglement sudden death and rebirth. This research demonstrates that specific non-classical features, including entanglement growth, decay, and birth, can be clearly identified and analyzed through the use of optical tomograms. Furthermore, these non-classical characteristics can be readily visualized and mapped using simple transformations of optical tomograms, making them accessible without the need for deeply technical measures such as Wigner functions. This research contributes to the development of a new framework for understanding and describing non-classical effects, even in cases where effects like entanglement's transformation from classical to non-classical, or vice versa, occur.

The measurement of the branching fraction for the $D^0 \to K^- \pi^+$ decay is determined to be $(3.94 \pm 0.05 \pm 0.08)\times 10^{-4}$, with the primary source of uncertainty being counting statistics, based on the relative branching fraction between $D^0 \to K^- \pi^+$ and $D^0 \to K^- \bar{K}^-$ decays. Additionally, the branching fractions for the $D^0 \to K^- K^- K^+$, $D^0 \to K^- \pi^- \pi^+$, $D^0 \to K^- \bar{K}^0 K^0$, and $D^0 \to K^- \bar{K}^0 \bar{K}^0$ decays are derived from experimental and theoretical data.

To reconstruct the lattice of submodules for a module acting upon it, beginning with a known set of composition factors, we focused on multiplicity-free modules. A distinct approach was needed when dealing with modules that have repeated factors. We developed a method that starts with the factor module itself and its corresponding action, proceeding to construct the lattice of submodules in a step-by-step process.

Repeated application of certain second-order elliptic operators can result in higher-order recurrent operators, and we examine how this property affects the conditions under which biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space are minimal.

A novel generalised rational number system p/q is introduced and a new model for input strings is introduced called p/q words. Within this framework, we offer a new definition for automata called p/q automata and a new definition for languages that can be recognised by these automata, referred to as p/q recognisable languages. Furthermore, we offer a concise geometric interpretation for p/q recognisable subsets that are subsets of the natural numbers and provide a characterisation of such subsets similar to the Biham-Waiter theorem. Additionally, we offer a novel Gaussian elimination algorithm for determining the parameters defining intervals that constitute a p/q recognisable subset of the natural numbers. Extending this algorithm, we provide a method for determining the parameters defining the intersection of p/q recognisable sets and the pre-image of a p/q recognisable set under the p/q projection map.

This paper compares the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert (CLN) and the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed (BGL) frameworks that parse $K\to\pi\pi$ decay rates. While both methods rely on the same basic principles, they result in distinct predictions due to different applications of the analytic constraints on the decay amplitude. A detailed comparison reveals that the discrepancies between the frameworks can be bridged through a revised set of input data, yielding consistent outcomes when utilizing the CLN approach, the BGL approach, and the combined BGL-CLN method that incorporates all admissible inputs. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the BGL framework accommodates the $\Delta I = 1/2$ rule within one standard deviation when employing all acceptable inputs, yielding a result of (2.00^{018}_{-022}) within the BGL approach, BGL theoretical predictions, and experimental data. Conversely, while the CLN framework accommodates the $\Delta I = 1/2$ rule with one standard deviation under all conditions, the BGL framework requires entry-level precision beyond what is currently achievable through BGL predictions and experimental data alone, necessitating a significant revision of the 12% precision of the K_2\to\pi\pi decay rate measurement to meet this criterion.

Dynamical systems exhibiting a positive Lyapunov exponent are considered to be in a state of chaos, as demonstrated by our findings for our proposed quantum chaotic system within the Rabi model under certain conditions. Our calculation method involves decomposing the phase space of quantum states into discrete segments and tracking their evolution over time, particularly in relation to their overlap with the initial state. Our results show that in a regime where the system exhibits chaotic behavior, the initial state's characteristics become increasingly prominent as the system progresses.

This study investigates certain negative curvature graphs and networks, extending the concept developed by M. Gromov and A. Vilhjammar. The primary goal involves resolving problems concerning conformal capacity, function spaces, and conformal embedding within these structures. Notably, new results emerge demonstrating that certain structures, specifically constant curvature graphs with deep trees and networks with uniform degrees but varying curvature, are conformally embeddable in 2-dimensional Euclidean space. Conversely, it is proven that networks with non-uniform degrees but consistent curvature, as well as specific structures with gradual increases in branching, cannot be conformally mapped within these structures. Additionally, a formula for calculating the conformal capacity of structures with two distinct endpoints is presented.

Recent efforts to protect point cloud models from malicious alterations are influenced by various simplifications and approximations, leading to less reliable guarantees. Specifically, existing theoretical frameworks protecting these models are vulnerable to certain transformations like rotation and scaling but not more complex transformations like twisting. Building on this discussion, our proposed TPC framework eliminates these limitations providing rigorous guarantees against twisting transformations while maintaining ease of implementation. Applying this framework to various point cloud models demonstrates its capability to certify accuracy against twisting transformations with higher fidelity compared to previous frameworks. Consequently, our method enhances the security of deep learning models by providing more accurate guarantees against twisting transformations and setting the basis for future research endeavors.

Software developers frequently utilize computer systems to identify and correct mistakes, but these tools often contain bugs that can hinder their effectiveness. Our unsupervised learning-based tool AToM aims to mitigate this issue by assisting in detecting and fixing defects within the tool itself. Since these defects are embedded in deeply complex environments, we created a novel automated testing framework to help identify them. When a tool bug is discovered, the environment can provide feedback to aid in fixing it, yet this process can be impeded by defects in the tools themselves. We devised a breakthrough algorithm to overcome and resolve these issues, which has been successfully integrated into numerous open-source tools including Bazel, Blackduck, and SonarQube. Our AToM system demonstrates its efficacy by successfully identifying previously unknown defects within these tools that the testing environment could verify.

G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles can be obtained by reducing certain crystalline extensions modulo p, and we demonstrate that this process does not lose too much information, leading to a near bijective relationship after a further reduction. Consequently, g_K-Artin-Scheier coordinates can establish the flat structure of varieties defined over finite fields. Additionally, we establish that variety definitions over finite fields preserving the flat structure are equivalent to those defined by g_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

This research explores the use of genetic algorithms (GA) to enhance neural network (NN) training for detecting and locating damage in self-sensing composite materials. The NN model is built upon data collected from fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensors embedded within the material. Initially, the network struggles with accurate damage detection due to the noise inherent in the material's constitutive modeling process, which links material deformation to electrical resistance changes. By integrating a CR gauge linearization step and utilizing FBG strain readings, the materials' behavior can be more accurately predicted. However, to further refine the model's response and enhance damage detection and localization capabilities, a standalone GA-driven optimization process is employed to fine-tune the resistance-strain relationship. A notable improvement in FBG sensor signal reconstruction and a notable 90% reduction in MSE between predicted and measured signals were achieved after this optimization step. Notably, the enhanced model demonstrates the ability to accurately detect and localize various types of damage, including single and multiple impacts, as well as delamination, by analyzing changes in the FBG sensor signals.

This paper introduces a novel approach to proving integral identities using vector geometry, presenting the method through several examples including Green's first and second identities, the divergence theorem, and the generalized Stokes theorem. By employing simple geometric vectors, we derive these fundamental theorems of vector analysis and explore their extensions and variations, discussing applications and potential future research directions. A supplementary video provides a visual overview of the vector geometry proved in this work.

We examine the action of a specific subgroup of a right-angled Artin group on a tree that results in a finite number of points remaining fixed and a linear number of segments increasing as the group size expands. This particular subgroup is formed by taking the direct product of two subgroups corresponding to a pair of subgraphs that divide the original graph into separate parts. We further demonstrate that these subgroups formed from different pairs of subgraphs dividing the original graph into separate parts are also distinct.

This paper focuses on accelerating the Nested Neumann algorithm for solving large-scale linear systems Ax=b, particularly when the matrix A is symmetric, positive definite but potentially ill-conditioned. A key factor influencing the algorithm's convergence rate is the chosen inception depth parameter. We introduce a adaptive strategy to optimize this parameter and conduct theoretical analysis on its performance. Furthermore, we integrate the accelerated version with the ELR preconditioning technique, creating a sophisticated, multi-level nested algorithm. Experimental results on several test cases validate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

We examine the role of prior knowledge about context distribution in accelerating learning processes for contextual linear bandit problems. Specifically, we compare two approaches: one with full knowledge of the context distribution and another with limited information, assuming the context space is discrete. Under certain conditions, we demonstrate that an algorithm called VolToContextFree can be adapted with minimal additional communication between the learning agent and supervisor. Notably, these extra bits required are negligible compared to other parameters, and we provide theoretical bounds on them. Additionally, we offer improved performance guarantees for various measurement scenarios, both with and without prior knowledge. Our findings build on existing research, showing that context distribution awareness primarily impacts sample complexity, largely failing to impact time and space complexity.

To effectively reduce temperatures in protoplanetary disk regions beyond a couple of astronomical units, minimal dust growth is required, and significant cleaning might be unachievable without substantial particle development and/or metallicity enhancement. A highly detailed radiative-convective equilibrium model has been presented and incorporated into a existing N-body code used for simulating protoplanetary disks. Our investigation into the influence of various factors, including initial dust size distribution, growth rate, and planet formation efficiency, indicates that, without substantial particle development, low densities in the disks' surfaces prevent efficient cooling and prevent N-body gravitationally driven instabilities. However, if dust growth to millimeter-scale particles is efficient or if metallicity is elevated, disks can develop cool, dense mid regions and warm, underdense surfaces, which align with observed disks and facilitate N-body collapse and fragmentation into numerous clumps that further divide through turbulent gas re-fragmentation. Ultimately, significant planet formation could occur in these cooled disks, or if dust growth is inefficient, clouds can settle in the mid region of the disk where higher densities facilitate growth and development of larger particles, enhancing cooling efficiency and facilitating N-body instability.

This paper focuses on a model of a manifold with a curvature tensor that decreases over time and extends previous findings by Li and Schoen that apply to harmonic functions on such manifolds. A key outcome of our research demonstrates that if a harmonic function on such a manifold does not grow excessively, its growth rate is bounded. Moreover, we establish a decomposition theorem for such functions that are polynomial in nature. This theorem implies that the space of such functions can be divided into a finite number of components that behave linearly, and the dimension of this space is invariant under transformations by the affine group SO(n). This dimension is closely related to the asymptotic behavior of the curvature tensor that decreases over time.

Neural network classifiers trained for multiple categories can be manipulated with a specific hidden pattern to trigger desired outcomes, even in advanced situations where the deception changes continuously or adapts based on the input. Although effective, such adaptable backdoor attacks are computationally expensive and hard to implement, especially in scenarios involving complex movements or behaviors. We introduce a straightforward method that enables fast execution of these attacks across numerous real-world image classification models including ResNet, DenseNet, and Inception. Our technique works seamlessly whether the target actions are static or involve complicated sequences and behaviors, and our implementation requires almost no extra computational resources, making it applicable to any model using the softmax method to classify inputs. Against several common image classification networks, our approach achieves remarkable success rates of 99.36%, 99.52%, and 99.71% with minimal errors of 0.00%, 0.08%, and 0.12% when utilizing sequence attacks on datasets like CIFAR-10, STL-10, and FashionMNIST, respectively, with a background setup that takes under a minute.

This research introduces a novel, decentralized algorithm for coordinating machine learning models across devices with vast amounts of data, eliminating the need for points of aggregation. A random walk mechanism facilitates device-to-device communication, progressively moving the model through the network. Key improvements over existing methods are achieved by slightly extending random walk approaches and better assessing their efficiency. Laboratory tests show that these enhanced methods nearly match centralized learning performance, despite the model's journey through the network, and significantly outperform current decentralized algorithms with minimal modification.

Recent advances in medical image segmentation have greatly reduced the need for annotation, with methods like self-training, contextual training, and label propagation showing promise. However, research on combining these techniques and developing new ones has been hindered by the lack of a framework do so. This paper introduces an innovative, theory-backed context called "interim contextual training" to facilitate the blending of existing techniques and developing new ones. Building on the foundations of contextual training and leveraging the power of interpolation-based methods, this context provides guidance on creating effective combination strategies, offering theoretical guarantees and recommended approaches do so. The authors evaluate these strategies using various techniques and evaluate them on multiple datasets, demonstrating the benefits of blending and providing insights into the characteristics that contribute to successful blending.

A nonlocal phenomenon and a quantum effect known as steering have been observed in single-particle systems through the use of entanglement between parts of a quantum system that consists of just one particle. A scheme is presented where continuous-variable quantum entanglement between two samples of a single particle results in the instantaneous transmission of quantum information between them over short distances, without the need for coordination. This process, which combines single-particle entanglement and its nonlocal properties with the correlation between different parts of the quantum system, can lead to closer quantum correlations than what single-particle entanglement can achieve on its own. Consequently, the application of nonlocality and the single-particle entanglement enables the instantaneous transmission of information between two locations without the need for instantaneous communication. This finding contradicts the idea that single-particle entanglement has limited potential for enhancing quantum information protocols when considering long distances.

The integration of the Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) and the blockchain (BC) technologies aims to resolve critical issues of security and privacy within IoVs systems. This study conducts a thorough analysis of the blockchain technology framework, detailing its key components, properties, renowned models, and widely accepted protocols. Subsequently, the paper explores various BC applications, demonstrations, and implementations within IoVs systems, as well as the utilization of smart contracts for enhancing these systems. Moreover, the authors propose several breakthrough directions for the synthesis of BC and IoVs technologies, illustrate the challenges and obstacles that need to be addressed, and suggest potential solutions. By presenting comprehensive surveys on BC and IoVs technologies, this work contributes significantly to guiding and accelerating the development of novel BC-enhanced applications, demonstrations, and implementations within the realm of IoVs systems.

This research introduces a novel hybrid hard tensor LSTM model that integrates the advantages of deep learning and advanced tensor techniques for language processing tasks. Our optimized hardware design, leveraging a streamlined tensor decomposition approach, significantly reduces the resource requirements for hardware implementation while maintaining high performance. We developed a custom FDHT-LSTM architecture and evaluated its throughput, accuracy, and energy efficiency through extensive simulations using realistic datasets. Compared to traditional tensor-decomposed models, our design demonstrates substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency, with gains of over two orders of magnitude in some cases, with minimal precision loss. Furthermore, we created an automated framework for optimizing the parameters of the FDHT-LSTM model and evaluated various optimization strategies to determine the most effective approach. Our proposed design outperforms state-of-the-art hardware implementations, setting new records in terms of throughput, accuracy, and energy efficiency, with notable achievements including 90.5% accuracy on the WikiQA dataset, throughput of over 100 MBps, and energy efficiency of over 100 tokens/Joule on the EMNIST dataset.

We resolve the bateman-horn conjecture for function fields, proving that for any finite subset of irreducible polynomials over the constant field in a given function field, there exists a polynomial in the function field that results in an extension where all given polynomials are no longer irreducible. Additionally, we explore the Galois group distribution in function fields and introduce a concept of natural density for subsets of the function field. The research is supported by the cognitive nature of the function field and the existence of the derivative operator enabling parameter integration.

This research focuses on the Schrödinger equation's solutions in a bounded region with a concave boundary, demonstrating that solutions can become unbounded under specific initial conditions that satisfy certain conditions related to the boundary and its curvature. Unlike previous findings, which were applicable to infinite domains or required reflective boundaries, this work is set within a bounded domain. The proof involves extending solutions across the boundary using the curvature and employing a localization technique, along with known results about solutions in infinite domains, to show the potential for blow-up behavior.

We extend results from characteristic zero to positive characteristic using the Emery-Chevalley theorem, with a brief overview of the recent proof of the Ax-Kochen/Ershov transfer theorem by Cluckers, Halupczok, and Van Dieren. This discussion builds on our earlier work on integrating semi-algebraic functions in positive characteristic, performed via the Ceresa-Hrushovski "cellular" technique. This approach allows us to handle both algebraic and geometric aspects seamlessly.

The paper addresses the challenge of making informed decisions when the target concept is uncertain and the cost of inquiries varies based on the current hypothesis. Building on Angluin's (1988) work, we propose a generic framework for active learning that accommodates any utility function guiding the learning process. A key finding is that in the absence of information about the target concept, the most effective strategy is to prioritize inquiries that maximize expected utility. To validate this optimal approach, we apply it to various learning scenarios, including character recognition, geometric shape identification, and navigating uncertain landscapes. Moreover, we introduce a novel method for determining the optimal strategy in cases where the target concept is a path within a graph.

Discourse markers play a crucial role in connecting ideas within text, yet analyzing their meanings is challenging due to the varied contexts in which they appear. Our DiscSense dataset addresses this challenge by focusing on descriptive and explanatory discourse relations, excluding other types of relations. Compiled from parallel English-French Wikipedia articles, our 10k sample is the most extensive available in a multilingual setting, with an annotated label system that bridges the gap between monolingual and multilingual contexts. We've developed a three-way classification model for DiscSense using a BERT-based approach, achieving an average accuracy of 82.1% in a test set, demonstrating the potential of our data in training both single-language and multi-language systems. Furthermore, we've initiated a resource for understanding the meanings of discourse markers, starting with an initial survey of English descriptions and explanations.

We extend the Jordanian deformation symmetry to constant fields varying linearly in time, demonstrating its equivalence to previously established results in non-constant scenarios. Initially introduced in 2010 by Dressera et al., this linear time-dependence consideration is shown to be equivalent to simpler versions of the Jordanian twist when fields are not constant. Additionally, we examine the consistency of this specific field configuration with Bethe-Salpeter and S-matrix symmetries, as well as a generalized Liouville theorem. Our findings indicate that the generalized twist remains compatible with these fundamental principles, even when considering time-varying, linear time-dependence, except for the Bethe-Salpeter symmetry in the case of non-constant fields. Furthermore, we briefly explore the generalized Arnold magnetic twist under these conditions.

We develop a systematic method to verify if one regular expression is included within another. This approach builds on two key operators: one that computes the language described by the union of regular expressions and another that computes the complement of a regular expression when it's a standalone expression. This operator was initially proposed by W. Brzozowski in 1959 and recently re-examined and implemented in a fully symbolic decision procedure. This procedure requires no conversion of regular expressions into automata and only uses simple text-based operations. We've created a Python library, ReXDec, that executes this procedure and is available for use at https://github.com/SebastienRouault/ReXDec. Our findings show that while the proposed method is theoretically sound, it may be more suitable for expressions that are not overly complex, as demonstrated by benchmarks comparing it to other approaches that use automata.

We examine the properties of boundary operators corresponding to geodesics within the AdS$_{2}$ hemisphere when applied to conformal field theory in two spacetime dimensions (CFT$_{2}$). By utilizing the global AdS$_{2}$ picture, we demonstrate that OPE blocks associated with conserved currents, specifically electric and magnetic charges, can be precisely represented by these AdS$_{2}$ geodesic operators. We also explore the behavior of multiple geodesic operators placed near the ideal point of the AdS$_{2}$ hemisphere's boundary and find that their correlation function asymptotically matches that of conformal primary operators in the context of the CFT$_{2}$. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between these operators and the Witt shift, a method for generating non-degenerate vacuum states within the Hartle-Hawking spectrum.

A lobster-eye optics system is a novel type of X-ray telescope that uses a spherical mirror design to enable a wide field of view and uniform imaging capabilities. This lobster-eye system includes a central, rounded module and four additional modules arranged in a cross shape around it.
